University of Artificial Intelligence lijie.hu@mbzuai.ac.ae ABSTRACT Agent skills, structured procedural knowledge packages injected at inference time, are increasingly used to augment LLM agents on software engineering tasks. How- ever, their real utility in end-to-end development settings remains unclear, and no standard procedure tests an individual skill before installation. We present SWE-Skills-Bench, a skill-centric, requirement-driven benchmark that measures how much individual agent skills improve performance on real-world software engineering (SWE) tasks. We start from 98 public SWE skills, each paired with a real GitHub repository pinned at a fixed commit. For each skill, we derive repository-specific requirements, create executable verifiers, and build a repro- ducible environment. Under each of four agent–model configurations, we run every task once without the skill and once with it, yielding 3,920 paired evaluations. For each requirement, we compute a paired delta, i.e., the change in outcome when the skill is added. We then aggregate these deltas across a skill’s ten requirements into a per-skill utility profile, and use a statistical test to classify each skill as Golden

nts, create executable verifiers, and build a repro- ducible environment. Under each of four agent–model configurations, we run every task once without the skill and once with it, yielding 3,920 paired evaluations. For each requirement, we compute a paired delta, i.e., the change in outcome when the skill is added. We then aggregate these deltas across a skill’s ten requirements into a per-skill utility profile, and use a statistical test to classify each skill as Golden (significantly helpful), Ineffective (no significant effect), or Harmful (significantly detrimental). Our results show that skills provide limited benefits: 92 of 98 skills have no statistically significant effect, and adding skills raises the average pass ratio only from 76.6% to 76.9%. The few helpful skills supply procedures that the agent would otherwise omit (gains of up to +17.7 points). In contrast, harmful skills anchor the agent on their own templates and override the task’s explicit instructions (losses of up to −17.0 points). We therefore reverse-engineer repository-specific requirements from each skill’s claimed procedures, then systematically translate their acceptance criteria into deterministic verifiers. Building on this principle, we presentSWE- Skills-Bench, a skill-centric framework for constructing and conducting automated evaluations of 2 software engineering skills. We manually curate 98 public SWE skills and pair each with an authentic GitHub repository pinned at a fixed commit. For every skill–repository pair, our pipeline (i) reverse- engineers ten skill-triggering requirements, (ii) synthesizes requirement-driven executable verifiers, (iii) constructs a reproducible Docker environment for the target repository, and (iv) conducts matched skill-free and skill-assisted executions across agent–model configurations. Because the paired arms differ only in whether the skill is available, the resulting change in pass ratio can be attributed to the tested skill under that configuration. Our work addresses this gap by constructing a requirement-driven benchmark focused exclusively on SWE, pairing each skill with fixed-commit repositories, explicit requirements, and deterministic, execution-based verification. 3 SWE-SKILLS-BENCH: REQUIREMENT-DRIVENSKILLEVALUATION 3.1 OVERVIEW ANDPROBLEMFORMULATION SWE-Skills-Bench evaluates a skill by measuring how much it improves the agent’s performance on requirements, which are reverse-engineered from the skill content. The input is a manually curated skill–repository pair (s, Rs), where Rs is an authentic GitHub repository pinned at a fixed commit. Once the skill and its repository are fixed, we proceed in three steps. First, we reverse-engineer repository-specific requirements from the skill’s content. Second, we build executable verifiers for these requirements and a reproducible environment for running them. Third, we run each requirement twice, once with the skill and once without it. None of these treats a skill as the intervention under test. The closest work is SkillsBench (Li et al., 2026), which evaluates agents with and without skills on 87 expert-contributed tasks across eight domains, using containerized environments and deterministic verifiers. However, SkillsBench istask-centricbut notskill-centric: each evaluation starts from a fixed, expert-contributed task and asks whether providing curated skills for that task improves agent performance. Furthermore, SkillsBench is not specifically designed for software engineering: software engineering is only one of its eight domains, and its primary goal is to measure broad cross-domain skill efficacy rather than requirement satisfaction in real-world development workflows.
